title: Laboratory safety rules
competency: Follow laboratory safety rules and explain why each rule matters.

keywords.def: A place where science experiments are done.
Rules that lower the risks of lab work, such as tying back hair and never tasting chemicals.
Items you wear to protect yourself in the lab, such as goggles, gloves, a lab coat and boots.
A strong acid with very little water in it.
A memory aid: A = acid, W = water. Add acid to water, never water to acid.

en.text: A laboratory is a place of learning. It can also be dangerous without the right care. So follow the safety rules. Dress properly and tie back hair. Know where safety equipment is. Never taste or smell chemicals. Do not eat or drink in the lab. Do only the experiments your teacher gives.

am.text: ቤተ ሙከራ የመማሪያ ቦታ ነው። ጥንቃቄ ካልተደረገ ግን አደገኛ ሊሆን ይችላል። ስለዚህ የደኅንነት ሕጎችን ተከተል። በትክክል ልበስ፣ ፀጉርህን እሰር። ኬሚካል አትቅመስ፣ አታሽትት። በቤተ ሙከራ ውስጥ አትብላ፣ አትጠጣ።

screens.title: Lunch in the lab?
screens.text: Dawit is in the school lab in Hawassa. He is hungry. He takes out his kolo and wants to eat it at the bench.
screens.ask: What do you think could go wrong?
opts: Chemicals could get into his food
The kolo could break the glassware
The teacher will just be angry
screens.after:
Lab benches and hands can carry traces of chemicals.
They can get onto food and be swallowed.
Some chemicals are poisonous.
That is why there is no eating or drinking in the lab. Read the rules.
screens.best: Chemicals could get into his food

screens.title: 1.2.2 Laboratory safety rules
paras: A laboratory is a place of discovery and learning. But lab work can also be dangerous.
Danger comes when the right precautions are not taken. Follow these rules in the lab.

screens.title: The safety rules
paras: Dress properly: goggles, gloves, shoes and lab coat. Tie back loose hair.
Know where safety equipment, like the fire extinguisher, is kept. Know what to do in an accident.

screens.title: Dress and prepare
items: Wear them to guard your eyes.
Wear them to guard your hands.
Wear proper shoes to guard your feet.

screens.title: More safety rules
paras: Do not taste or smell chemicals. Do not eat or drink in the laboratory.
Do only the experiments your teacher assigns. Dispose of all chemical wastes properly.
screens.note: Never add water to concentrated acid. Always add acid to water.

screens.title: Rules and protection
defs: Rules that lower the risks of lab work, such as tying back hair and never tasting chemicals.
Items you wear to protect yourself: goggles, gloves, a lab coat and boots.

screens.title: Spot the rule
screens.ask: Which of these is a laboratory safety rule?
opts: Taste a little to identify the chemical
Work alone when your teacher leaves
Do not eat or drink in the laboratory
screens.ans: Do not eat or drink in the laboratory
screens.why:
Step 1: check each option against the rules.
Step 2: tasting and smelling chemicals are forbidden.
Step 3: you do only the experiments your teacher assigns, so no working alone.
Step 4: "Do not eat or drink in the laboratory" is a rule.
So that is the answer.

screens.title: Why each rule matters
paras: Protective clothing guards you from spills, splashes and heat. Loose hair can catch fire or fall into chemicals.
In an emergency there is no time to search for equipment. Knowing the accident steps lets you act fast.

screens.title: Why protective clothing?
screens.ask: Why do we wear goggles, gloves, closed shoes and a lab coat?
opts: To protect our eyes, hands, feet and clothes from hazards
screens.ans: To protect our eyes, hands, feet and clothes from hazards
screens.why:
Step 1: in a lab, chemicals can spill or splash, and glass can break.
Step 2: goggles guard your eyes; gloves guard your hands.
Step 3: closed shoes guard your feet; a lab coat guards your clothes and skin.
So we wear them to protect ourselves from hazards.
Looking like a scientist is not the reason.
screens.clue: What can spill, splash or break in a lab?

screens.title: Near the flame
screens.ask: Safety near a flame: before you work near a Bunsen burner, tie back loose ___.
screens.why:
Step 1: a Bunsen burner has an open flame.
Step 2: loose hair can swing into the flame and catch fire.
Step 3: it can also fall into chemicals.
So you tie back loose hair.
screens.clue: What on your head could catch fire?

screens.title: Why the other rules matter
paras: Many chemicals are poisonous or harm your lungs. They could also get into food or drink.
Your teacher has checked that assigned experiments are safe. Careless waste harms people and the environment.

screens.title: Rule and reason
screens.ask: Tap each rule to see why it matters.
items: Wear goggles, gloves and a lab coat
They guard your eyes, hands and clothes from spills, splashes and heat.
Loose hair can catch fire or fall into chemicals.
In an emergency there is no time to search.
Do not taste, smell, eat or drink
Many chemicals are poisonous. They could get into food or drink.
Your teacher has checked that they are safe.
Careless waste harms people and the environment.

screens.title: The teacher steps out
screens.text: The teacher leaves the lab for a few minutes. Meron wants to mix two chemicals to "see what happens".
opts: Mix them quickly before the teacher returns
Do only the experiment the teacher assigned
Ask a friend to mix them
screens.ans: Do only the experiment the teacher assigned
screens.why:
Step 1: the rule: carry out only the experiments your teacher assigns.
Step 2: the teacher has checked those experiments are safe.
Step 3: two unknown chemicals can react, get hot or give poisonous gas.
So Meron does only her assigned experiment.
Smelling them first breaks another rule too.
screens.clue: Which rule is about which experiments you may do?
screens.worked:
Step 1: the rule says: do only the experiments your teacher assigns.
Step 2: mixing chemicals "to see what happens" is not assigned.
Step 3: it could be dangerous.
So Meron waits and does only her assigned work.

ideas.name: Add acid to water: AW! Not WA!

en.text: Never add water to concentrated acid. Always add acid to water. Remember the Amharic "AW! Not WA!": A is acid, W is water. Water poured into strong acid can heat up and splash out. Acid added slowly to water is safer.

am.text: በተከማቸ አሲድ ላይ ውሃ በፍጹም አትጨምር። ሁልጊዜ አሲድን ወደ ውሃ ጨምር። "አው! ዋ አይደለም!" አስታውስ፤ A አሲድ ነው፣ W ውሃ ነው። ውሃ በጠንካራ አሲድ ላይ ሲፈስ ሊሞቅና ሊረጭ ይችላል።

screens.title: Which goes first?
screens.text: A teacher in Gondar must make a strong acid weaker. She will mix it with water.
screens.ask: Which way do you think is safer?
opts: Pour the acid slowly into water
screens.after:
Mixing strong acid and water gives off a lot of heat.
If water goes into acid, the little water boils at once and acid splashes out.
If acid goes slowly into lots of water, the water soaks up the heat.
Read the rule to check your guess.
screens.best: Pour the acid slowly into water

screens.title: Acid into water
paras: Never add water to concentrated acid. Always add acid to water.
Remember the Amharic "AW! Not WA!" (A = acid, W = water).

screens.caption: Pour acid slowly into water. Never water into acid.

screens.title: Why acid goes into water
paras: Water poured into strong acid can heat up and splash out. It can burn you.
Acid added slowly to water is safer.

screens.title: Diluting an acid, step by step
steps: Put on goggles, gloves and a lab coat.
Pour the water into the beaker first.
Add the acid slowly, a little at a time.
Stir gently so the heat spreads out.
Never pour the water into the acid: AW! Not WA!

screens.title: The AW rule
defs: A strong acid with very little water in it.
A = acid, W = water. Add acid to water, never water to acid.

screens.title: Dilute it safely
screens.ask: What is the correct way to dilute a concentrated acid?
opts: Pour both together at the same moment
Add the acid into the water
screens.ans: Add the acid into the water
screens.why:
Step 1: the rule is "AW! Not WA!".
Step 2: A = acid, W = water. Acid goes into water.
Step 3: water into acid can heat up and splash out.
So add the acid into the water.
"It does not matter" is wrong: the order matters for safety.
screens.clue: Remember the Amharic AW! Not WA!

screens.title: Finish the rule
screens.ask: Diluting acid: always add ___ to water. Never add water to concentrated acid.
screens.why:
Remember "AW! Not WA!".
The first letter, A, stands for acid.
Acid goes into water.
So the missing word is acid.
screens.clue: In "AW", what does the A stand for?

screens.title: True or false?
screens.text: Diluting acid: pouring water into concentrated acid is safe if you pour slowly.
screens.why:
Step 1: the rule is never water into concentrated acid.
Step 2: the first drops of water meet a lot of acid and get very hot.
Step 3: they can boil and splash acid out, even if poured slowly.
So the statement is false. Always acid into water.
screens.clue: Which goes into which: A into W, or W into A?
screens.worked:
Step 1: the rule is "AW! Not WA!": acid goes into water.
Step 2: water into acid can heat up and splash out.
Step 3: pouring slowly does not make it safe.
So the statement is false.

screens.title: Safe or unsafe?
screens.text: Is each action safe or unsafe in the lab?
items: Hair can catch fire or touch chemicals.
Taste a chemical to find out what it is
Add acid to water, not water to acid.
Eat your lunch in the lab
No eating or drinking in the lab.
Learn where the fire extinguisher is
You must know where safety equipment is.
Try your own experiment while the teacher is out
Do only the experiments your teacher assigns.
Wear goggles and a lab coat
It can splash and burn. Remember: acid into water.
All chemical waste must be disposed of properly.
screens.why:
Step 1: for each action, find the rule it follows or breaks.
Step 2: safe: tie back hair, acid into water, know where the fire extinguisher is, wear goggles and a lab coat, dispose of waste properly.
Step 3: unsafe: tasting chemicals, eating in the lab, your own experiment, water into acid.
Each safe action follows a rule. Each unsafe action breaks one.
screens.clue: For each action, find the rule in the list it follows or breaks.

test.text: Safety rules: it is safe to taste a chemical to find out what it is.
test.why:
The rule says: do not taste or smell chemicals.
Many chemicals are poisonous.
Even a small taste can harm you.
So the statement is false.

test.text: Why must you tie back loose hair in the lab?
opts: It could catch fire or touch chemicals
test.ans: It could catch fire or touch chemicals
test.why:
Loose hair can swing into a Bunsen burner flame and catch fire.
It can also fall into chemicals.
Looking neat is not the reason; safety is.
So the answer is: it could catch fire or touch chemicals.

test.text: To dilute a concentrated acid, you should:
test.why:
The rule is "AW! Not WA!".
A = acid goes into W = water.
Water into acid can heat up and splash.
Heating or smelling the acid is never part of diluting.
So add the acid to water.
